newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria delays deposit compensation in ailing banks.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria delays deposit compensation in ailing banks.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament on Tuesday decided to delay payment of compensation for personal and company deposits in bankrupt banks to avoid a fresh rise in state spending.

"Under amendments to the Deposit Guarantee Law approved by parliament, citizens' deposits in insolvent banks will be fully repaid by the state no sooner than 30 days after the court declares the banks insolvent," said a parliament press officer.
Companies would be able to draw their lev deposits from insolvent banks 60 days after the ruling.
So far compensation payments have begun immediately after the central bank filed an insolvency suit to the courts.
The law provided for a 100 percent state guarantee on personal savings in those banks and 50 percent coverage of companies' deposits.

Under the new amendments, personal foreign exchange deposits in bankrupt banks will be compensated in four semi-annual tranches, but the first instalment will be paid six months after the court rules on those banks' insolvency.

Under the law, the government issued treasury bonds worth a total of 80 billion levs and $100 million, which were placed with the State Savings Bank and the state-owned Bulgarian Post Bank to guarantee payments to depositors in the five banks.
The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) has filed insolvency suits against five local banks since May in line with bank stabilisation pledges made to multilteral lenders.
Regional courts postponed rulings on the five banks' insolvency for November and December pending further investigation of their financial state.
Opposition deputy Muravei Radev criticised the amendments, saying that their value will be completely eroded by inflation. Monthly inflation averages at around 15 percent this year.
The BNB placed a further nine state-owned and private banks under special supervision last month to establish their state and decide whether to seek their insolvency through courts.
